title: Third-party Google resource classification
description: Classifies Google resources loaded by websites that are not Google. Blocking a request stops it before it leaves the machine, so Google never receives the IP address, user agent, referring page or any fingerprinting surface. This goes further than cookie separation, which only stops the request carrying an identity.

notes.why-tiers: Facebook Container can block every Meta resource on other sites because almost nothing on the web depends on Meta code loading. Google is not comparable. Fonts, hosted script libraries, reCAPTCHA and embedded maps are load-bearing for a large share of the web, so blocking them by default would break sites rather than protect people. Tracking resources have no such excuse and are blocked by default.
notes.cookies: Blocking is separate from containment. Even an allowed resource cannot read the Google container's cookies, because it loads in the host page's own compartment.

notesTracking: Analytics, advertising and attribution. These exist to observe people and have no function the host page needs. Blocked by default on sites that are not Google.
notesSocial: Share buttons, follow widgets and similar embeds. Mostly cosmetic, so they are blocked by default, but the YouTube player API is excluded from blocking through functionalPaths because removing it leaves a dead video player rather than a missing button.
notesFunctional: Resources the host page genuinely needs: web fonts, hosted script libraries, embedded maps and videos, reCAPTCHA, sign-in, translation and Firebase back ends. Allowed by default. Strict mode blocks these too and will visibly break sites, which is why it is opt in and carries a warning.
notesFunctionalPaths: Path prefixes that are load-bearing even on a host that is otherwise classified as tracking or social. Checked before the host classification, so apis.google.com/js/api.js keeps working while the rest of apis.google.com stays blocked.
notesNeverBlock: Blocked in no mode at all, including strict. Removing these takes away the ability to log into a site or submit a form, which locks people out of their own accounts. A privacy tool that does that has failed. Scoped to the specific sign-in scripts rather than all of apis.google.com, so legacy share widgets on that host are still blocked.
